figure: C8
ours: How far the forest's AUC drops when the column is shuffled, on loans it did not train on. AUC is the chance a random bad loan scores above a random good one; 0.5 is a coin flip. The development loans are cut into 3 runs by date; each run is scored by a forest grown on the other two, with 5 shuffles of each column, and the drops are averaged. The forest's own AUC is 0.628. ours: A random forest: 200 trees, each leaf at least 40 loans, seed 7, grown by scikit-learn 1.9.1. AUC is the chance a random bad loan scores above a random good one: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1 is perfect. Built is the forest's AUC on the development loans, each scored by a forest grown on the others (the Scouting tab); unseen is on the held-back loans. Unseen well under built means the tree learnt those years, not the book. Said twice: from the candidates alone, and with FICO and CHANNEL in the forest too.

ours: One logistic regression on the held-back loans with every candidate's groups in it at once, each against its own reference, and one constant for each pocket FICO and CHANNEL make, so the pockets are held fixed as they are below. Each odds ratio is then net of every other candidate. Adds is a likelihood ratio test of taking the candidate out, all its groups at once: its test statistic, on as many degrees of freedom as it has groups less one, and its p-value, after the allowance for testing the shortlist at once. Adds? is Yes when that p-value is under the bar. Moves with names candidates whose values rise and fall together (a rank correlation of 0.7 or more, on the development loans): what one adds, the other may already say. The loans are the held-back ones with a value of every candidate, in pockets where some went bad and some didn't.

ours: The odds ratio against its reference group. Odds are bad loans divided by good ones, and an odds ratio is a group's odds divided by its reference group's: 2.00× means twice the odds of going bad. While few loans go bad it is close to how many times as often they do. Worked out by conditional logistic regression, which compares the groups inside each pocket and takes each pocket's own count of bad loans as given, instead of estimating a rate for every pocket, which biases the answer when pockets are thin.

ours: Under the chart, one block per candidate. Does each candidate matter at all: the general test (the Mantel-Haenszel test for its groups: a standard way to add pockets up without mixing their loans), read against a chi-square on one fewer degree of freedom than its groups; the trend test, which gives the groups the scores 1 to their number and asks whether the bad rate climbs or falls steadily with them, on 1 degree of freedom; and the regression's block test (a likelihood ratio test, on one fewer degree of freedom than its groups), whether the groups together add anything. A difference with no trend is a U or a hump, which a straight-line test would call nothing. Then each group's odds ratio with its range and its raw p-value, before any allowance, and how much of the held-back loans' losses sit in each group (on the holdout only, and on the book as a whole, not pocket by pocket: the lift, the group's bad rate over the holdout's, is the finding, never the share of all losses).
note: the analyst's answer or a fixed setting, shown back

ours: The trend test scores each candidate's groups 1, 2, 3 and on, evenly spaced, rather than by where their numbers sit. Conditional logistic regression is used in every pocket, whatever its size: the unconditional fit the scope allows for pockets over a few thousand loans isn't used, as the conditional one is exact and quick at any size. A loan with no readable value in a column the pockets are cut by sits in a pocket of its own, as on the grids. A group with no bad loan, or only bad loans, in the pockets that say something has no odds ratio; the others are fitted as if its loans weren't there, which is where the regression heads anyway. Excess is scaled to the whole book by its losses over the held-back loans' losses. The allowance treats each set of loans as one family, every candidate's groups together, as a grid's pockets are one family per rate. All together gives each pocket its own constant rather than conditioning the pockets out, and refuses when they average under 5 bad loans each (statistics.md B10).
